paragraphs: A protein’s function often depends on the range of shapes it can adopt. This paper develops models that generate collections of plausible structures from a protein sequence. The aim is to represent its conformational landscape: the structural variation that a single predicted shape cannot capture.

The authors adapt AlphaFold and ESMFold, which predict individual structures, by fine-tuning them with a custom flow matching framework. The resulting models, AlphaFlow and ESMFlow, generate structures conditioned on sequence. In training and evaluation using the PDB, the approach offers a better combination of precision and diversity than AlphaFold with MSA subsampling.

Additional training on ensembles from all-atom molecular dynamics enables the method to capture flexibility, positional distributions, and more complex ensemble properties for unseen proteins. It can also generate variation around a static PDB structure, reaching certain equilibrium properties faster in wall-clock time than replicate molecular dynamics trajectories. These findings support its potential as a proxy for expensive simulations, with the speed claim specifically tied to those properties.
icml-2024-alphafold-meets-flow-matching-.tldr: AlphaFlow and ESMFlow adapt protein structure predictors into generative models that capture structural ensembles and can accelerate estimation of certain equilibrium properties.

paragraphs: Prompt learning can represent a new visual concept through a learned text embedding that functions like a new word. A harder problem is separating several unfamiliar objects within one scene. Existing approaches that crop or mask objects can require prior knowledge of the concepts and substantial manual effort.

Multi-Concept Prompt Learning learns several unknown words together from a single sentence-image pair, without image annotations. Its central challenge is associating each learned word with the appropriate visual concept. The method introduces three regularizers—Attention Masking, Prompts Contrastive Loss, and Bind Adjective—to strengthen those associations and refine attention boundaries.

Quantitative comparisons involving real-world categories and biomedical images show that the method can learn concepts with distinct semantic meanings. This matters because representing multiple objects separately makes the learned words more informative than an undivided representation of a scene. The approach learns only textual embeddings and uses less than 10% of the storage required by the compared methods, combining concept separation with a compact learned representation.
icml-2024-an-image-is-worth-multiple-wor.tldr: MCPL learns multiple distinct object concepts from one sentence-image pair without image annotations, using compact textual embeddings.

paragraphs: Learning complex manipulation from demonstrations requires connecting individual actions to the larger sequence of skills that completes a task. This paper addresses that problem using demonstrations that may be suboptimal. Its approach learns both the actions to perform and intermediate guidance describing how the task should progress.

The method first discovers subskills without supervision through an approach that does not depend on a particular observation space. It groups actions that are close in time and similar in function. Observations at the boundaries between these groups form a sequence of planning steps, which the authors call a chain of thought.

A Transformer then predicts this sequence as guidance for action generation. Learnable prompt tokens and a hybrid masking strategy connect action and subskill predictions, allowing the guidance to change during execution. Across the tested challenging manipulation tasks, Chain-of-Thought Predictive Control consistently outperforms strong existing baselines using suboptimal demonstrations. The findings support learning an explicit, updateable intermediate plan as a useful component of generalizable low-level control.
icml-2024-chain-of-thought-predictive-co.tldr: CoTPC learns subskill sequences from imperfect demonstrations and predicts them alongside actions to improve manipulation policies.

paragraphs: Instrumental variables are used to estimate causal effects, but choosing an instrument does not automatically resolve uncertainty about causation. Without additional assumptions, such as linear relationships, the available evidence may not determine a unique causal effect. The paper addresses this difficulty by seeking bounds on the effect.

The proposed bounding method operates under weak confounding. Its goal is partial identification: restricting the possible causal effect to a range rather than necessarily recovering one value. This distinction matters because a useful causal conclusion can describe which effects remain possible even when exact identification is unavailable.

The paper also addresses whether a proposed instrument can be ruled out. Observational data typically cannot establish the relevant causal graph, making instrument validity difficult to test. The authors introduce a falsification criterion that uses side information about the confounder. This provides a way to reject an instrument under the criterion, rather than a general certification of validity. Simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the utility of the proposed approach.
icml-2024-conditional-common-entropy-for.tldr: The paper bounds causal effects under weak confounding and uses side information about confounders to help falsify proposed instrumental variables.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether predicting code tokens can lead a language model to represent what programs do. The authors train a Transformer on synthetic programs for navigating two-dimensional grid worlds. Each program is preceded by a partial specification consisting of several input-output states, while training remains focused on next-token prediction.

They examine hidden representations with a probing classifier that attempts to recover intermediate grid states never shown explicitly in the training examples. As training progresses, these states become increasingly recoverable. This provides evidence that the model develops representations related to program execution, suggesting an emergent ability to interpret programs in this controlled setting.

A central methodological issue is whether the probe uncovers information already represented by the model or learns the relevant computation itself. The authors introduce an interventional baseline to distinguish these possibilities. The contribution is an experimental framework and evidence about semantic representations, rather than a new training technique. They suggest the intervention method may also help other semantic probing studies.
icml-2024-emergent-representations-of-pr.tldr: Controlled experiments suggest that next-token training can produce internal representations of program execution, supported by an intervention-based probing framework.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across devices while keeping their data local. A difficulty is client drift: local training can pull updates in different directions, harming performance and increasing communication. This paper studies how to reduce communication without making each device’s computation unnecessarily expensive.

The authors revisit DANE, an existing distributed optimization method. They show that it can deliver the desired reduction in communication when the local objectives satisfy Hessian similarity constraints, which concern similarities in their curvature. They then introduce DANE+, allowing arbitrary approximate local solvers and more flexibility in combining updates from devices.

The final method, FedRed, uses doubly regularized drift correction to improve local computational complexity while retaining the communication complexity of DANE and DANE+. The contribution therefore separates two costs that matter in distributed training: how often devices communicate and how much work they perform locally. The stated communication result for DANE depends on the Hessian similarity constraints, so it should be understood within that setting.
icml-2024-federated-optimization-with-do.tldr: FedRed improves local computational complexity while preserving DANE-style communication complexity through doubly regularized drift correction.

paragraphs: Combining federated learning with self-supervised learning creates an objective mismatch. The desired global self-supervised objective usually differs from the weighted sum of objectives computed independently on devices. Consequently, averaging locally trained models does not precisely minimize the global objective, which can hurt representation quality when devices have different data distributions.

FedSC addresses this problem using a spectral contrastive objective. Alongside model weights, clients periodically share correlation matrices describing their learned representations. These summaries enable comparisons across clients as well as the comparisons and contraction performed within each client, bringing information about separate datasets into the representation-learning process.

Sharing additional summaries also introduces additional privacy exposure. FedSC applies differential privacy to control leakage from the correlation matrices, and the paper analyzes both convergence and this extra leakage. Numerical experiments support the algorithm’s effectiveness. Its contribution is a principled way to address the global-objective mismatch while explicitly accounting for the privacy implications of the extra information exchanged.
icml-2024-fedsc-provable-federated-self-.tldr: FedSC shares privacy-protected representation correlations to support cross-client contrastive learning and better address the federated self-supervised global objective.

paragraphs: Combining visual modalities can provide complementary information, but the way a model combines them affects both accuracy and cost. The authors find that replacing less informative tokens with features from another modality underperforms cross-attention. Cross-attention, however, becomes computationally demanding when the input contains many tokens.

GeminiFusion exploits aligned representations to combine modalities at the pixel level. It brings together attention within a modality and attention between modalities, allowing complementary information to influence the result dynamically. Layer-adaptive noise controls how these two forms of attention interact at different layers of the network.

The method’s computational complexity grows linearly with the number of input tokens, supporting efficiency comparable to networks that use a single modality. Evaluations cover image-to-image translation, three-dimensional object detection, and semantic segmentation with modalities including RGB, depth, LiDAR, and event data. The reported improvements over leading methods support the value of using alignment to make multimodal interaction efficient while preserving useful exchanges between information sources.
icml-2024-geminifusion-efficient-pixel-w.tldr: GeminiFusion combines aligned modalities through pixel-level attention with linear token complexity and reports improvements across several vision tasks.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes geometric structure in the final features and classifier weights learned by deep classification models. Much existing work considers settings with relatively few classes compared with the number of feature dimensions. This paper investigates the opposite regime, where many classes must be represented in a lower-dimensional feature space.

The authors characterize a generalized collapse phenomenon in which the smallest one-versus-rest margin is maximized. In plain terms, the geometry emphasizes the weakest separation between a class and its alternatives. This extends the study of learned feature structure to settings relevant to language models, retrieval systems, and face recognition.

The paper provides empirical evidence that this generalized structure appears in practical neural networks. It also proves occurrence within an unconstrained feature model subject to a spherical constraint and technical conditions relating feature dimension to class count. The empirical observations and conditional theoretical result serve different roles: one establishes practical occurrence in the studied networks, while the other explains it within a specified mathematical setting.
icml-2024-generalized-neural-collapse-fo.tldr: The paper extends neural collapse to many-class settings, finding margin-maximizing geometry empirically and proving it under specified model conditions.

paragraphs: Serving a large language model can be expensive when computation is concentrated in a single datacenter. HexGen investigates distributed inference across different GPUs and datacenters, where both device capabilities and network connections vary. The practical challenge is assigning work so that this uneven infrastructure can still meet latency requirements.

The inference engine supports asymmetric partitioning through both tensor model parallelism and pipeline parallelism. This allows different portions of the computation to be assigned unevenly across devices. A scheduling algorithm formulated through constrained optimization adapts those assignments to the available GPUs, network conditions, and inference requests.

The authors evaluate HexGen while serving Llama-2 with 70 billion parameters. At the same budget, the results suggest it can achieve latency deadlines up to 2.3 times lower or tolerate request rates up to four times higher than a homogeneous baseline. These are alternative reported operating improvements, showing how flexible scheduling can turn heterogeneous resources into useful serving capacity.
icml-2024-hexgen-generative-inference-of.tldr: HexGen schedules uneven inference workloads across heterogeneous GPUs and datacenters, improving reported latency or traffic capacity at a fixed budget.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle to count structural patterns such as cycles, limiting the functions they can learn. One response is to add pattern counts to graph features. Existing approaches use either subgraph counts or homomorphism counts, which encode structural information through different kinds of pattern relationships.

This paper argues that both approaches are suboptimal in a particular sense when they do not use the full collection of relevant basis structures. The proposed alternative incorporates homomorphism counts for every structure in the target pattern’s basis. The key idea is that a richer set of related counts can expose distinctions that a coarser pattern description misses.

The authors prove that this construction yields strictly more expressive architectures without increasing computational complexity relative to existing approaches. They develop results for motif quantities defined at both node and whole-graph levels, then validate the theory on standard benchmarks. The result links a more careful choice of structural features to stronger representational power, while preserving the stated complexity level.
icml-2024-homomorphism-counts-for-graph-.tldr: Using homomorphism counts for all structures in a target pattern’s basis strengthens graph-network expressiveness without increasing the stated computational complexity.

paragraphs: A semantic identifier aims to encode something about a document or item’s meaning in its ID. Common methods first obtain text embeddings and then convert them into identifiers. Both stages can lose information, and the embedding distribution may be poorly matched to the structure needed for indexing.

LMIndexer learns semantic identifiers using a generative language model. It addresses the difficulty of producing discrete, sequential IDs through progressive training and contrastive learning. This brings semantic representation and hierarchical identifier structure into the same learning framework, rather than relying entirely on representations produced for a separate purpose.

Because direct semantic supervision is limited, the framework learns through a self-supervised document reconstruction objective. Reconstructing the document supplies a training signal for what the identifier should preserve. Evaluations across recommendation, product search, and document retrieval on five datasets show high-quality learned IDs and demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution is a unified approach to learning identifiers whose structure carries useful semantic information across several retrieval-related tasks.
icml-2024-language-models-as-semantic-in.tldr: LMIndexer learns structured semantic IDs with a generative language model, using document reconstruction and contrastive learning to support retrieval-related tasks.

paragraphs: Language models often struggle when their input is longer than the sequences seen during training. SelfExtend explores whether an existing model can handle longer contexts through changes to inference alone. The authors argue that useful long-context capabilities are already present and can be accessed without fine-tuning the model.

The method constructs two levels of attention using the model’s original self-attention mechanism. Grouped attention captures relationships between tokens that are far apart. Neighbor attention handles relationships among nearby tokens within a specified range. Together, these mechanisms account for both distant context and local connections.

SelfExtend requires only minor code modifications and no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that it can effectively extend the context windows of existing language models. The contribution is therefore an inference-time strategy for making longer inputs usable with an already trained model. The findings support the proposed attention construction on the evaluated benchmarks without establishing that every model can process arbitrarily long inputs equally well.
icml-2024-llm-maybe-longlm-selfextend-ll.tldr: SelfExtend expands language-model context windows without fine-tuning by combining grouped attention for distant tokens with attention over nearby tokens.

paragraphs: A common way to build a vision-language model is to convert a vision encoder’s output into visual prompts placed in a language model’s input. Even when only a small portion of the model is fine-tuned, those prompts increase input length. This creates an efficiency cost during both adaptation and use.

Memory-space visual prompting, or MemVP, introduces visual information through the language model’s feed-forward networks. The approach draws on the view that these networks act as key-value memories. It concatenates visual prompts with their weights, treating the visual information as additional knowledge available to the model when solving a task.

This changes where visual conditioning enters the model and addresses the input-length overhead of conventional visual prompting. Across the evaluated vision-language tasks and language models, MemVP substantially reduces training time and inference latency while outperforming previous parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. The findings indicate that the location of visual information inside the architecture can matter for both computational efficiency and downstream task performance.
icml-2024-memory-space-visual-prompting-.tldr: MemVP injects visual prompts through language-model feed-forward weights, reducing reported training time and inference latency while improving task performance.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are attractive for energy-efficient, fast inference, but their binary spikes make gradient-based training difficult. Surrogate gradients help address this issue. When combined with back-propagation through time, however, training requires storing intermediate information across all time steps, creating substantial memory demands and obstructing online learning.

NDOT uses the temporal sensitivity inherent in neuronal dynamics to compute gradients while moving forward through time. It decomposes the full gradient into temporal and spatial components. This makes the neurons’ evolving dynamics central to tracking how earlier activity affects learning, rather than requiring the usual backward traversal across time.

The authors explain the intuition through Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, an algorithm that explicitly uses historical information. NDOT plays a similar role by capturing temporal dependencies through neuronal dynamics. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR10-DVS report superior performance with few time steps. These results support the approach across both static-image and neuromorphic datasets, connecting online training with effective use of temporal information.
icml-2024-ndot-neuronal-dynamics-based-o.tldr: NDOT uses neuronal dynamics to track temporal dependencies and train spiking networks forward in time, with strong reported results using few time steps.

paragraphs: Group averages can conceal differences in how a classifier distributes its predictions. Even a measure covering the entire prediction distribution can hide a large disparity concentrated near particular prediction values. This paper develops a fairness measure designed to identify such extreme local differences when assessing demographic parity.

The proposed MCDP metric examines cumulative ratio disparities as prediction neighborhoods vary and focuses on the largest local discrepancy. This shifts attention toward the part of the prediction range where groups differ most strongly. The authors provide a provably exact calculation method as well as an approximation that greatly reduces computational complexity while keeping estimation error low.

They also develop a bi-level training algorithm using a differentiable approximation of MCDP, allowing the metric to influence model learning. Experiments on tabular and image datasets report superior fairness-accuracy trade-offs. The contribution therefore covers both diagnosis and intervention: detecting localized disparities and incorporating that concern into training, with the reported benefits evaluated through the paper’s fairness framework.
icml-2024-on-the-maximal-local-disparity.tldr: MCDP measures extreme local prediction disparities between groups and supports a training method with improved reported fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

paragraphs: Research on language models has suggested that high-level semantic concepts are represented linearly in their internal representation spaces. This paper asks where that structure comes from. Its focus is an explanation of how the training process can produce the observed organization of meaning inside a model.

The authors introduce a latent variable model that formalizes how underlying concepts participate in next-token prediction. This abstraction provides a mathematical setting in which the relationship between concepts, prediction, and representation geometry can be studied. Within that formalism, they prove that linearity follows from the loss function together with the implicit bias of gradient descent.

The result connects the shape of learned representations to both what training optimizes and how optimization proceeds. It gives a theoretical account of linear semantic structure within the proposed model, rather than merely documenting that structure after training. Experiments provide further empirical support for the theory. Together, the analysis and evidence offer an explanation for why next-token learning can favor linear representations of concepts.
icml-2024-on-the-origins-of-linear-repre.tldr: A latent-variable theory links linear semantic representations to the next-token loss and gradient descent’s implicit bias, with empirical support.

paragraphs: Time series analysis helps people understand systems through measurements that change over time. The authors argue that much current modeling depends heavily on domain expertise and extensive tuning, with prediction receiving most of the attention. They propose a broader research direction centered on the potential capabilities of large language models.

This position paper presents language models as a possible foundation for more general time series analysis. The envisioned capabilities include question answering and switching between time series and other modalities. Such capabilities could expand the role of a model beyond producing forecasts toward supporting interpretation and decision-making across a wider range of tasks.

The paper discusses integration with existing language-model technologies and identifies promising research directions. Its claims concern potential and an agenda for future work: general time series analytical intelligence remains at an early stage. The authors encourage researchers and practitioners to engage with these efforts and build trust in them. The contribution is a perspective on what the field could pursue, rather than a reported demonstration that this broader intelligence has been achieved.
icml-2024-position-what-can-large-langua.tldr: This position paper argues that language models could broaden time series analysis beyond forecasting toward question answering and more general analytical capabilities.

paragraphs: Many protein models based on three-dimensional structure emphasize residues, often represented through alpha carbon atoms. This leaves out other atomic details, including side chains, that can matter for downstream tasks such as molecular docking. The paper investigates how to learn useful representations at both residue and atom levels.

Simply combining these levels can fail during pre-training. The authors identify information leakage as a key reason: atomic structure in the input can reveal enough information to make residue-level training tasks trivial. A model can therefore complete the training task without developing sufficiently expressive residue representations.

The proposed solution masks spans along three-dimensional protein chains during pre-training. This strategy is intended to prevent the shortcut while supporting meaningful learning at both levels of detail. Experiments on binding-site prediction and function prediction show significant improvements over other methods. The findings emphasize that adding structural detail is not sufficient by itself; the training task must make both residue and atom representations informative.
icml-2024-pre-training-protein-bi-level-.tldr: Span masking addresses information leakage in protein pre-training, enabling useful residue- and atom-level representations with improved prediction results.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems whose objective nests several smooth functions inside one another, with decisions restricted to a closed, convex set. It focuses on stochastic, projection-free methods. Existing methods had weaker sample-complexity results and analyses concentrated on non-convex objectives and a single measure of optimization progress.

The authors introduce variance-reduction algorithms and analyze them using multiple criteria. Under the gradient-mapping criterion, their sample complexities improve previous results and match optimal rates for unconstrained problems. Under the Frank-Wolfe gap criterion, the guarantees align with those available for single-level optimization, despite the nested objective structure.

A stage-wise adaptation extends the analysis to convex and strongly convex objectives. This broadens the theoretical coverage beyond the non-convex setting and makes the guarantees relevant to different kinds of objective geometry. Numerical experiments on several tasks support the methods’ effectiveness. The main contribution is a stronger collection of complexity guarantees, showing that nested stochastic objectives can be handled without the previously reported gaps under the stated criteria.
icml-2024-projection-free-variance-reduc.tldr: New projection-free variance-reduction methods strengthen complexity guarantees for nested stochastic optimization across several objective classes and progress criteria.

paragraphs: Biomedical tables often contain many features but relatively few examples. Choosing useful features is therefore central to learning from them. Methods that select features separately for each example can overlook features that matter across the dataset, and the selection and prediction components can suffer from co-adaptation.

ProtoGate balances global and local feature selection adaptively to choose features for individual examples. It then makes predictions through a non-parametric prototype mechanism. The design aims to address co-adaptation while keeping selected features and predictions consistent with the clusters present in the data.

The authors evaluate both predictive performance and interpretability using synthetic and real-world datasets. ProtoGate generally exceeds state-of-the-art prediction accuracy by a clear margin and provides high-fidelity feature selections and explainable predictions. The qualified finding is that it generally performs better across these evaluations. Its contribution connects two forms of explanation—identifying relevant features and using prototypes for prediction—within a model designed for data with many dimensions and few samples.
icml-2024-protogate-prototype-based-neur.tldr: ProtoGate combines adaptive global-to-local feature selection with prototype-based prediction to improve accuracy and interpretability on small, high-dimensional biomedical datasets.

paragraphs: Flexible sensors offer a wearable and privacy-preserving route to motion capture with few restrictions on natural movement. Training existing deep-learning systems, however, requires large, varied labeled datasets. Collecting these in specialized motion-capture studios takes equipment and manual labor, making scale difficult and expensive.

The paper proposes transferring from simulation to reality for hinge-joint tracking, drawing on the high linearity of flexible sensors. Its SuDA method aligns the supports of predictive functions across source and target domains. This changes the target of adaptation from matching instance-dependent distributions to matching the supports associated with the prediction functions.

The resulting approach eliminates the need for labeled data in the proposed tracking solution while achieving accuracy comparable to supervised learning. Extensive experiments also show an advantage over leading distribution-based domain-adaptation methods for this task. The findings support support-based alignment as a useful way to bridge simulation and real sensing in the hinge-joint setting, where the sensors’ linear behavior motivates the approach.
icml-2024-suda-support-based-domain-adap.tldr: SuDA transfers hinge-joint tracking from simulation to reality through predictive-function support alignment, reporting supervised-comparable accuracy without labeled data.

paragraphs: Expert-generated tables can contain valuable information for image classification, yet collecting that information can be expensive. This paper considers using such tables during learning so that predictions can later rely on images alone. The challenge is identifying which tabular attributes correspond to visual information and transferring them appropriately.

Charms aligns image channels with tabular attributes using optimal transport. It compares similarity distributions across the two modalities to select relevant information, especially morphological characteristics. This selective alignment matters because the usefulness of a tabular attribute depends on its relationship to the visual features available to the classifier.

The method also maximizes mutual information between image channels and tabular features, extracting knowledge from both numerical and categorical attributes. Experiments show improvements in image-classifier performance and interpretability. The contribution is a way to retain useful expert knowledge in an image-based predictor even when the accompanying table is unavailable at inference. The reported benefits come from making the correspondence between tabular expertise and visual representations part of learning.
icml-2024-tabular-insights-visual-impact.tldr: Charms transfers relevant expert tabular knowledge into image classifiers, improving reported performance and interpretability when tables are unavailable at inference.

paragraphs: Extending image-text language models to video requires representing both visual appearance and change over time. Video-LaVIT addresses this challenge by decomposing a video into keyframes and temporal motion. This separates two kinds of information that must be captured for effective video-language pre-training.

Specialized tokenizers convert the visual and motion information into a small number of discrete tokens. These tokens allow videos, images, and text to participate in a unified generative training framework built around a language model. During generation, the model’s output tokens are converted back into continuous pixel representations to produce video content.

The framework supports both understanding and generation of images and videos. Across 13 multimodal benchmarks, it achieves competitive performance on these capabilities. The contribution is a shared modeling approach in which a compact representation of appearance and motion makes video compatible with language-model training and generation. The benchmark results support the usefulness of this decomposition across the evaluated understanding and content-generation tasks.
icml-2024-video-lavit-unified-video-lang.tldr: Video-LaVIT represents keyframes and motion as discrete tokens to jointly train a language model for image and video understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Correcting a deployed language model’s errors can make it fail on examples learned earlier. Replaying randomly selected earlier examples can help, but the authors describe its performance as unsatisfactory, variable, and difficult to control. They investigate predicting which specific examples an update will cause the model to forget.

Forecasting models are trained on collections of newly learned examples paired with earlier examples subsequently forgotten. One partially interpretable approach uses similarities in changes to pre-softmax scores. It performs reasonably on BART but fails on T5, showing that this forecasting mechanism does not transfer successfully across the studied model families.

A black-box classifier based on inner products between example representations forecasts forgetting more effectively across several setups. The authors then replay examples predicted to be at risk and show reduced forgetting of upstream pretraining examples. This connects forecasting to a practical intervention: choosing replay data according to anticipated damage from an update. The findings support targeted replay while preserving the distinction between the more interpretable method and the better-performing black-box approach.
icml-2024-what-will-my-model-forget-fore.tldr: Forecasting which earlier examples a language-model update will break enables targeted replay that reduces forgetting in the reported experiments.
